hero.name: Rafiq
hero.who: an app-cab driver in Mumbai whose mind never stops buzzing with news and worry

story.b: Rafiq drives his cab across Mumbai twelve hours a day. The radio plays breaking news, his phone buzzes with group messages and forwards, and the navigation voice keeps announcing turns. Between rides, he scrolls through his cousin's photos from Dubai: a new car, a big flat. At night, at home in Kurla, he cannot sleep. His mind replays the car loan EMI, his daughter's school fees and an argument with his brother from two years ago. His wife says he looks tired even on holidays. Rafiq feels like his head never goes quiet. One evening he snaps at a passenger over a small route change, then feels ashamed all the way home.

ask.q: Rafiq's mind never goes quiet, even at night. Where is the best place for him to start?
o: Cut down the news and messages that pour into his head all day
Drive extra hours so he is too tired to think at night
Ignore it, since every driver lives with this noise
ask.why: Extra hours only add exhaustion, and accepting the noise as normal changes nothing. Much of his restlessness comes from what he lets in all day. Choosing fewer inputs is a simple, practical first step toward a calmer mind.

chapters.take: A calm mind begins with what you let into it.

story.b: Rafiq makes a few changes. He turns off the news radio and plays old Hindi film songs, or nothing at all. He leaves five forward groups and keeps only the drivers' group, muted, which he checks during his lunch break near Bandra station. He reads the news once a day, over cutting chai, and then puts the phone in the glove box. The first two days feel strange. He keeps reaching for the phone at every signal. By the end of the week, the silence in the cab starts to feel like space rather than emptiness. He notices the sea at Worli for the first time in months. Passengers seem less annoying, though they have not changed at all.

ask.q: Another driver says he must follow every news update or he will fall behind. What could Rafiq tell him?
o: Turn on more alerts so he never misses anything
Stop reading news entirely and forever
Check news once a day at a fixed time, and enjoy the quiet otherwise
ask.why: More alerts mean more noise and less room to think. Cutting news forever is extreme and hard to keep. A fixed, once-a-day check keeps him informed while protecting the rest of his day, much like choosing what and when to eat.

chapters.take: Be as choosy about information as you are about food.

story.h: A notebook by the kitchen light
story.b: One night at 1 am, Rafiq is wide awake, worrying about money again. Instead of tossing in bed, he gets up quietly, takes a thin notebook his daughter used for rough work and writes in Hindi by the kitchen light. EMI due on the fifth. School fees due in March. Then he writes what he can actually do: two extra airport rides each week, and asking the school about paying fees in parts. It takes ten minutes. The worry that felt like a mountain now looks like a list with three items. He goes back to bed and falls asleep within half an hour. The next night, Rafiq writes again, just five minutes, before lying down.

ask.q: Rafiq's friend lies awake at night going over the same worry. What simple step would help most?
o: Scroll on his phone until he feels sleepy
Write the worry and possible next steps in a notebook before bed
Keep thinking until he solves it fully in his head
ask.why: Scrolling adds more noise to a busy mind, and circling the worry in his head keeps it huge and vague. Writing it in plain words slows the thoughts down and often shows the problem is smaller and more manageable than it felt at midnight.

chapters.take: A worry written down usually looks smaller than it felt.

story.b: Even with less noise, something still pulls at Rafiq. Every time his cousin Salim posts from Dubai, Rafiq feels a sting. Why does Salim get the big car while he sits twelve hours in traffic? He also still carries a grudge against his brother over a loan from two years ago. One evening, he does something unusual. He sends Salim a warm message saying the new flat looks lovely and that he is happy for him. Salim calls back, delighted, and admits he badly misses Mumbai and his family. On Sunday, Rafiq visits his brother with a box of sweets. They do not talk about the loan. They talk about their mother. Rafiq sleeps well that night.

ask.q: Rafiq's friend keeps comparing his income with a richer classmate's and feels bitter. What would bring him the most peace?
o: Let go of the comparison, practise gratitude and wish the classmate well
Work harder until he earns more than the classmate
Unfollow everyone so he never sees anyone's success
ask.why: Racing to beat the classmate keeps the comparison alive, and hiding from everyone avoids the feeling without healing it. Letting go of envy, noticing what he is grateful for and wishing others well settles the heart, so it stops pulling him in many directions.

chapters.take: Envy and grudges keep a heart restless. Kindness lets it settle.

story.b: Rafiq sits for twelve hours a day, and his back aches. A regular passenger, a retired schoolteacher, mentions that she walks by the sea every evening to clear her head. So after his shift, Rafiq parks near Carter Road and walks for twenty minutes, without earphones. At first it feels like wasted time when he could be earning. But he notices the breeze, the smell of vada pav and the boys playing cricket near the rocks. His thoughts slow down. One evening, halfway through the walk, he suddenly sees an answer to his school fees worry: offering fixed morning airport rides to regular office customers. The best idea of his month comes on foot, not in the cab.

ask.q: Rafiq feels walking is a waste of earning time. What is the better way to see it?
o: Skip the walk and do two more rides instead
Walk only on holidays when there is nothing else to do
Treat a short daily walk as time that clears his mind and helps him think
ask.why: Two more rides add money but keep his body stiff and his mind cluttered. Holiday-only walks are too rare to help. A short, regular walk without earphones gives his body movement and his mind space, which is often when clear ideas arrive.

chapters.take: Moving your body is one of the simplest ways to quiet your mind.

story.b: The cab app keeps offering bonuses for late-night rides, and Rafiq has been saying yes to every one, even on Sundays. The drivers' group also pulls him into angry arguments about fares that go on for hours. He decides to leave some space. Sunday evenings are now for his family: no rides, no group. He takes his daughter to Juhu beach for bhel puri. When an argument starts in the group, he reads it and does not reply. Not every bonus is worth chasing, he decides, and not every fight needs his voice. His earnings drop a little. His temper drops a lot more. Rafiq feels sharper on Monday mornings than he has in years.

ask.q: Rafiq's brother wants to say yes to every extra shift and every family function. What advice fits best?
o: Say yes to all of it, since rest can come later
Guard some empty time each week and turn down what does not matter
Drop all family functions to focus only on work
ask.why: Saying yes to everything leaves no room to recover, and dropping all family time throws away what matters most. Guarding some empty time and declining the things that do not count keeps him rested and present for the moments that do.

chapters.take: Empty space in your week is not laziness. It keeps you sharp.

story.b: Weeks later, Rafiq's cab is quieter. The radio stays off most days, and the phone lives in the glove box between rides. He still worries sometimes, but the notebook on the kitchen shelf catches most of it before bed. He walks at Carter Road three or four evenings a week. Salim now calls every Friday, and Rafiq's brother came over for Eid with his children. Two office customers book his morning airport rides regularly, which covers the school fees. When a passenger is late and rude one evening, it does not ruin his day. Rafiq notices the irritation, lets it pass and drives on. His wife says he looks rested, even on a working day.

chapters.take: Stillness grows from small daily choices about what you let in.
